items.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
items.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

items.title: Inclusive co-design and AI devices: a new paradigm of pedagogical mediation for schools
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within Italian educational contexts represents one of the most complex digital transitions of the contemporary world (Han et al., 2022; Hopcan et al., 2023). Following the pandemic experience and the lockdown, schools have witnessed a proliferation of training offers for teachers, both curricular and specialized in support, often characterized by huge efforts. In this scenario, AI cannot be reduced to a simple instrumental innovation; in fact, it requires a profound redefinition of educational design and professional roles. Abandoning an initial technooptimism, international research today requires a critical-reflective approach: integrating these technologies without analyzing their ethical assumptions risks amplifying existing inequalities. As a result, the distinction proposed in the literature between an AI used "instead of education", which replaces the relationship, and an AI used "for education", which acts in support of human pedagogical goals, becomes fundamental (Holmes et al., 2022). items.title: INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND LEARNING ANALYTICS ON THE PERFORMANCE OF POSTGRADUATE STUDENTS IN UNIVERSITIES IN CROSS RIVER STATE
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: This study investigated the influence of artificial intelligence and learning analytics on the performance of postgraduate students in universities in Cross River State, Nigeria. The study specifically examined the influence of artificial intelligence technologies, ethical implications of artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and ethical implications of learning analytics on postgraduate students’ learning. Four research questions and four null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study was conducted in public universities offering postgraduate programmes in Cross River State. A sample of 300 postgraduate students was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving purposive, stratified random, and proportionate sampling procedures. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled *Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics Influence Questionnaire (AILAIQ)*. The instrument was validated by three experts in Educational Technology and Measurement and Evaluation, while a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained using Cronbach’s Alpha. Data collected were analyzed using simple linear regression to answer the research questions, while regression t-test was used to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that artificial intelligence technologies had a significant positive influence on postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 6.7% of the variance in learning outcomes (R = .259, R² = .067, t = 5.132, p < .05). Ethical implications of artificial intelligence also had a significant influence, accounting for 13.3% of the variance (R = .365, R² = .133, t = 7.512, p < .05). Learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, although its contribution was relatively small, accounting for 1.2% of the variance (R = .109, R² = .012, t = 2.107, p = .036). Similarly, ethical implications of learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 7.9% of the variance (R = .282, R² = .079, t = 5.627, p < .05). Based on these findings, the study concluded that artificial intelligence and learning analytics, as well as the ethical conditions surrounding their use, significantly influence postgraduate students’ learning in universities in Cross River State. The study recommended, among others, that universities should strategically integrate AI and learning analytics into postgraduate education, develop clear ethical frameworks for their use, strengthen digital infrastructure, and provide adequate training for lecturers and students on the responsible and effective use of these technologies. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, learning analytics, ethical implications, postgraduate students, academic performance, universities, Cross River State.

items.title: Information rather than architecture: cross-learner attribution and clinician–model complementarity in CIN2+ risk prediction for women referred for colposcopy
items.abstract: Background Deep tabular models, including self-supervised and pretrained foundation models, are increasingly proposed for clinical risk prediction, but their value over conventional learners is rarely tested against matched controls, and their role relative to clinician judgement is seldom examined. Methods In a retrospective single-centre cohort of 879 women referred for colposcopy (242 CIN2+, 27.5%), 15 routinely recorded variables, including a clinician image-based assessment documented before histopathology, were modelled with ten model families under one fixed protocol (single fold assignment and seed, no tuning). Discrimination was compared by paired DeLong tests and bootstrap. Two analyses were pre-specified: exact Shapley attribution of discrimination to five clinical groups of variables in every model family, and a complementarity analysis asking whether routine data identify CIN2+ among women judged negative by the clinician. Frozen models were evaluated in a 103-case two-centre external cohort. Results Out-of-fold AUROC ranged from 0.726 to 0.761. No model outperformed logistic regression (AUROC 0.757; CatBoost −0.002, p = 0.860; TabPFN +0.004, p = 0.554), and three matched ablations of a self-supervised tabular Transformer were null (all p ≥ 0.096). Removing the clinician assessment lowered AUROC in all ten families (by 0.041 to 0.072; all p ≤ 0.008). Shapley attribution ranked five variable groups identically in every family (Kendall’s W = 1.00; permutation p < 0.001): the clinician assessment (39% to 50% of discrimination above chance), then cytology, HPV testing, colposcopic findings and demographic history. The clinician assessment alone had sensitivity 0.504 and specificity 0.882; 49.6% of CIN2+ occurred in clinician-negative women. Re-reviewing the 20% of clinician-negative women with the highest model risk identified 34.2% (95% CI 25.7–42.7%) of the missed CIN2+, against 20% expected at random, raising pathway sensitivity to 0.674 at specificity 0.733. External AUROC of logistic regression was 0.710. Conclusions On routine structured data from a colposcopy-referral population, and under a common protocol, model architecture did not determine performance; predictor information did. Retrospectively, routine data complemented the clinician modestly in clinician-negative women, rather than replacing clinical judgement. Claims that complex architectures improve clinical tabular prediction should be tested against logistic regression with paired uncertainty across repeated data splits.

items.title: Inhabiting the Algorithmic Pulse: Affective Digital Literacy and Critical Citizenship in the Era of the Fourth Revolution
items.abstract: In the age of the Fourth Revolution, understood not only as the convergence of cyber -physical systems and artificial intelligence but also as a mutation of human self-understanding, the sharp distinction between online and offline dissolves into a constitutively hybrid "onlife" condition. Digital environments do not merely transmit information: they orchestrate emotional states, modulate attention and construct reputational identities, acting upon a subjectivity solicited from within rather than repressed from without. Setting out from Asimov's short story Evidence and the figure of the "maimed master", the essay locates the true terrain of the educational challenge not in computational power but in empathy and affectivity. The risk is not that machines will become human, but that humanity will grow accustomed to a synthetic affectivity, devoid of the weight of the body and of the responsibility inherent in relationship. items.title: Innovation in Education: India's Emerging Model, Government Initiatives, Challenges and Solutions.
items.abstract: Abstract Education is undergoing a significant transformation in response to technological development, changing social conditions, emerging employment opportunities and the increasing demand for practical and skill-oriented learning. In this context, innovation in education has become an important area of discussion in India. Educational innovation, however, should not be understood merely as the introduction of computers, smart classrooms or artificial intelligence. It includes changes in teaching methods, curriculum, assessment, classroom interaction, institutional practices and the relationship between education and society. The present paper examines the changing nature of educational innovation in India with particular reference to school and higher education. It analyses India's policy direction under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and discusses initiatives such as PM SHRI Schools, Atal Tinkering Labs, Frontier Technology Labs, digital education platforms, experiential learning and technology-enabled higher education. The paper also examines evidence from UDISE+ and the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 to understand the realities of educational development, particularly in rural India. ASER 2024 provides evidence on enrolment, foundational learning and, for the first time at national scale, digital access, usage and skills among children aged 14–16. The paper argues that India's emerging model of educational innovation is gradually moving from a technology-centred approach towards a broader model involving experiential learning, creativity, problem-solving, digital literacy, vocational exposure, holistic assessment and community participation. At the same time, challenges such as the digital divide, infrastructure limitations, teacher preparedness, unequal access and the tension between innovative pedagogy and conventional assessment continue to affect implementation. The study concludes that educational innovation becomes meaningful only when technology, teachers, students, curriculum and local context work together to improve actual learning.

items.title: Innovations and Challenges in Smart-Textile Wearables for Postural Monitoring: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: In many work environments, professionals perform physically demanding routines involving repetitive movements and prolonged static postures, increasing exposure to biomechanical risk factors associated with work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs). Wearable technologies offer opportunities for continuous posture monitoring and real-time feedback, but their occupational deployment remains challenging due to limitations related to comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and integration with work clothing. This scoping review aims to synthesize and critically analyze the existing evidence on smart-textile-based wearable systems for occupational posture monitoring. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and CINAHL was conducted, identifying 566 records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 34 studies were included in the final synthesis. The included studies were analyzed according to wearable architectures, sensing technologies, data processing and posture recognition, user feedback mechanisms, and energy management strategies. Hybrid architectures combining textile-based sensors and inertial measurement units, together with machine learning and real-time feedback, emerged as promising approaches for continuous posture monitoring. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical or laboratory validation, with relatively small samples and limited long-term evaluation in real occupational environments. Five studies reported changes in posture or ergonomic behavior following the use of the technology, while no direct evidence of reductions in WRMSD incidence or severity was identified. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial technological potential for smart-textile-based posture monitoring, but current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical or occupational effectiveness in preventing WRMSDs. Future research should prioritize prospective, long-term validation involving larger and more diverse worker populations under real-world occupational conditions, while addressing comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and compatibility with occupational clothing and personal protective equipment.

items.title: Innovative language teacher education approaches integrating ai-assisted models
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence within educational environments is profoundly reshaping language teaching. Language teachers are increasingly expected to operate in digitally mediated environments and to integrate technological tools into their pedagogical practice (Godwin-Jones, 2022). Yet resistance remains widespread. Without adequate training that addresses both the technical and pedagogical dimensions of AI use, hesitation is a predictable and, in many respects, rational response. The literature confirms that resistance to AI adoption stems from a structural deficit: limited preparation, insufficient theoretical grounding, and the absence of models that connect technological tools to principled language pedagogy (Godwin-Jones, 2022; Kovačić & Bubaš, 2023). This challenge is particularly acute in LSP education, where language learning is inseparable from disciplinary discourse, professional communication, and context-sensitive language use. Specialized discourse cannot be reduced to automated linguistic processing, and teachers who lack a robust pedagogical framework struggle to evaluate what AI tools can and cannot do within their specific instructional contexts. items.title: Institutional Governance Authenticity and Student Responses to Artificial Intelligence Assessment Guidelines in Higher Education
items.abstract: Abstract Rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities worldwide to issue guidelines on student AI use in assessment. While existing research catalogues policy content and student misuse, little is known about how students perceive these guidelines and how such perceptions shape behaviour. This paper argues that current research treats guidelines as a binary intervention—present or absent—overlooking their psychological and institutional authenticity. Drawing on procedural justice and neutralisation theories, we contend that when guidelines are vague, invisible, unenforceable, and treated by academics as box-ticking exercises, they fail as integrity safeguards and may instead provide justifications for disingenuous AI use. We further argue that this pattern reflects institutional compulsions—legal, reputational, and competitive—that drive guideline issuance despite known limitations. We propose a research agenda centred on guideline authenticity and its effects on fairness perceptions, moral neutralisation, and compliance intentions, alongside perceptions of institutional motivation. A sequential mixed-methods design is outlined, drawing on UAE and UK contexts. The agenda aims to move institutional practice beyond symbolic policy-making toward genuinely embedded academic integrity cultures.

items.title: Instructional Emotion in the Age of Artificial Intelligence：Value, Alienation Risks, and Pathways for Reconstruction
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence in education raises questions about how emotional experience, relational care, and professional responsibility can be sustained in increasingly data-mediated teaching environments. This conceptual article examines instructional emotion as an interrelated configuration of teachers’ emotional engagement, students’ learning-related experiences, and the affective relationships through which teaching acquires meaning. Drawing on scholarship on achievement emotions, caring pedagogy, teacher–student relationships, and artificial intelligence in education, the article organizes its analysis around three value foundations: embodied human experience, relational connection, and teachers’ professional responsibility. It then identifies four potential forms of alienation arising when technological efficiency overrides educational judgment: procedural rigidity in teaching methods, emotional distance in interaction, the loss of affective meaning in content, and the reduction of assessment to measurable performance. Corresponding reconstruction pathways include emotionally adaptive instructional design, humanistic interaction, affective knowledge graphs, and emotionally responsive assessment. These pathways are guided by teacher judgment and bounded by consent, fairness, transparency, and human oversight. The framework distinguishes the interpretation of emotional evidence from claims to measure learners’ inner states directly. Its contribution is to connect educational values, potential risks, and pedagogical responses within a coherent conceptual structure. The proposed relationships remain open to empirical examination across educational settings.

items.title: Instructors’ Perceptions of Microsoft Teams Reading Progress in an Omani EFL Foundation Programme: Adoption, Challenges, and Institutional Feasibility
items.abstract: Oman’s digitisation priorities under Oman Vision 2040 encourage the integration of technology into teaching and learning. Little research examines instructors’ perceptions of Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) Reading Progress in Omani General Foundation Programme (GFP) contexts, particularly regarding its pedagogical value, ease of use, and implementation challenges. This mixed-methods pilot study explored instructors’ perceptions of Reading Progress in General English 2 (GE2), within the pre-degree GFP at the Preparatory Studies Centre (PSC), University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Oman. MS Teams Reading Progress is an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported tool designed to help students practice reading aloud, improve accuracy and fluency, and give instructors performance data. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study explored instructors’ perceptions of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions, and behavioural intention. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from three sources: a structured questionnaire (N = 10), two semi-structured interviews, and MS Teams usage logs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed thematically. The findings reveal a disconnect between teachers’ positive perceptions and willingness to continue using the tool and students’ limited engagement. Although instructors believed the tool could support reading fluency and accuracy, its use remained low, possibly due to the timing of the pilot, the absence of continuous assessment (CA), and limited time within the course plan. The findings indicate that wider implementation would benefit from early rollout, integration into course design, and CA weighting.

items.title: Instrumented Charpy impact test: review and future directions
items.abstract: Abstract The conventional Charpy impact test provides a single primary measure of material performance: the total energy absorbed during fracture. When strain gauges or piezoelectric sensors are incorporated into the striker, however, the test can record force as a function of time and displacement throughout the impact. These measurements provide a more detailed picture of how a material responds and fractures under dynamic loading. The conventional Charpy impact test provides a single primary measure of material performance: the total energy absorbed during fracture. However, by incorporating strain gauges or piezoelectric sensors into the striker, the test can provide continuous force-time and force-displacement data throughout the fracture event, offering substantially more detailed information on the material’s dynamic fracture behavior. This review traces the development of the instrumented Charpy impact test from its early twentieth-century origins to its current applications. The fundamental principles underlying the measurement are described, with particular emphasis on the characteristic forces identified from the force-displacement curve and their physical significance. The final section of this review considers emerging works that may push instrumented Charpy testing further. Among the most promising directions are machine learning and artificial intelligence, digital twin technology, robotic automation, and high-speed digital image correlation (DIC).

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence With PPE: A Smart Boiler Suit Framework for Maritime Survey Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Marine surveyors are routinely exposed to complex hazards, chemical, ergonomic, and physical, within dynamic environments such as ships and offshore platforms. Existing personal protective equipment (PPE) provides only basic safeguards and remains largely reactive. This paper proposes the design and conceptual architecture of an AI‐enhanced smart PPE boiler suit specifically optimized for marine and offshore class surveyors. The proposed system is envisioned to leverage embedded sensor networks, edge/cloud artificial intelligence analytics, and real‐time communications for continuous hazard detection, predictive risk mitigation, and streamlined survey workflows. We detail a proposed system architecture, outline pathways for functional prototyping, and critically examine anticipated challenges, establishing a robust roadmap for future multidisciplinary research and industry adoption. No physical prototype has been constructed at this stage; all scenarios and performance figures presented herein are theoretical and intended to guide future empirical validation.

items.title: Interacting with stakeholders
items.abstract: We wrap up the discussion with a reflection on techniques how to interact with stakeholders. Within scientific software development, stakeholders involve intra- and extra-institutional colleagues on different career levels, maturity and with different intrinsic motivation. There certainly are further groups such as the general public or businesses. The present chapter narrows the discussion down to academic collaborators for which we discuss interaction techniques as opposed to scheduling from Section 14.8 . Even within this narrow focus, the list of techniques refrains from an attempt to exhaustively map and discuss the different stakeholder groups. Instead, some common communication techniques that have proven valuable are distilled, and the focus falls exclusively on interaction patterns as they affect day-to-day development work. The developer's point of view is prioritised.

items.title: Interdisciplinary evaluation of assistive technology
items.abstract: This white paper is the deliverable of work package 2.5 “Interdisciplinary evaluation protocols” (german: “Interdisziplinäre Evaluierungsprotokolle”) of the Center for Assistive Technologies Rhein-Ruhr (Zentrum Assistive Technologien Rhein-Ruhr, ZAT, see Wild-Wall et al. 2024). It addresses the evaluation of assistive technology (AT), which we define as any device, software, equipment, or system that enables people with disabilities, functional limitations or special needs to perform specific tasks. The purpose of evaluating AT is to assess, in a systematic and reproducible manner, how effectively it fulfills its intended function in close interplay with the human user(s). Because AT, by definition, interacts with people, its evaluation must account not only for technological performance but also for social and human factors. A meaningful and comprehensive evaluation therefore requires an interdisciplinary perspective, drawing on the methodological toolkits of multiple disciplines and approaches.

items.title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
items.abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.

items.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models
items.abstract: Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

items.title: Intervensi Suplemen Asam Lemak Omega-3 Terhadap Penurunan Keluhan Muskuloskeletal Disorders (MSDs) pada Penenun Ikat Tradisional di Kelurahan Fatubenao Kecamatan Kota Atambua Kabupaten Belu
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) are a major occupational health problem in the informal sector, particularly among traditional weavers who work in repetitive postures for extended periods. Traditional ikat weavers in Fatubenao Village, Atambua City, Belu Regency, experience significant musculoskeletal complaints due to prolonged awkward postures. This study aimed to analyze the effect of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in reducing musculoskeletal disorder complaints among traditional ikat weavers. A quasi-experimental study with a non-equivalent control group design was conducted on 30 respondents (15 intervention, 15 control). MSDs complaints were measured using the Nordic Body Map (NBM) instrument covering 28 body regions. Omega-3 supplementation was administered for 14 days. Data analysis used the Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test and Mann-Whitney Test. The highest MSDs complaints prior to intervention were found in left and right ankle (76.7%), lower back (73.3%), left wrist (70.0%), and left upper arm (63.3%). Wilcoxon test showed significant reduction in the intervention group (Z = -3.417; p = 0.001). Mann-Whitney posttest revealed a significant difference between intervention and control groups (U = 54.000; p = 0.014). Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for 14 days significantly reduced MSDs complaints among traditional ikat weavers. This non-pharmacological intervention is safe, affordable, and effective for controlling MSDs in informal sector workers. items.title: Interventions in Leisure, Self-Management and Youth Wellbeing: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This work presents a systematic review on self-management, leisure, youth and wellbeing, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Considering the long research tradition in leisure studies addressing youth wellbeing but the scarce evidence available on leisure-based interventions specifically promoting self-management and its favourable influences on non-vulnerable and vulnerable youth, the following research question was answered through this systematic review: what interventions or good practices in self-management of leisure have an impact on wellbeing among youth, both vulnerable and non-vulnerable youth? After applying the PRISMA 2020 protocol, several studies with strong relevance to the topic of study were reviewed, and the main findings were discussed. The discussion covers key topics addressed in the reviewed literature regarding self-management, leisure, youth and wellbeing outcomes, as well as features or types of interventions working on self-management with a greater contribution to youth wellbeing. In this regard, interventions satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness consistently yield higher intrinsic motivation and wellbeing; youth who independently organise leisure report higher satisfaction and emotional benefits; and team-based interventions outperform individual or sedentary pursuits in perceived wellbeing. Moreover, important gaps in the literature were identified so that future research can be oriented towards closing them, such as the age bias with a predominant focus on ages from 10 to 19 years, which leaves emerging adults (20–29) underrepresented; the short-term focus due to most studies measuring only pre-to-post outcomes instead of long-term impact with scarce follow-up data; and geographical and cultural gaps, as the literature is concentrated in Western cultures.

items.title: Islamic Ethics in the Digital Era: A Bibliometric Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has introduced complex ethical challenges that require critical examination through religious and moral perspectives, including Islamic ethics. This study aims to systematically map the intellectual structure, research development, collaborative networks, and emerging thematic trends in scholarly literature concerning Islamic ethics in the digital era. Employing a bibliometric approach, the study utilizes VOSviewer to conduct citation analysis, co-authorship analysis, institutional and country collaboration mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, overlay visualization, and density visualization. The findings reveal that Islamic digital ethics constitutes an increasingly interdisciplinary research domain encompassing artificial intelligence, digital communication, Islamic finance, blockchain, and sustainable digital transformation. Citation analysis identifies blockchain, financial technology, and Islamic finance as influential areas of scholarly contribution. The collaboration analysis demonstrates the prominent roles of Indonesia and Malaysia in international research networks, although institutional collaboration remains relatively concentrated. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies artificial intelligence, Islamic ethics, digital ethics, social media, and ethical principles as dominant themes. Furthermore, overlay visualization indicates a thematic transition from digital financial applications and communication technologies toward machine learning, digital transformation, and sustainable development. Density visualization confirms the concentration of scholarly attention around artificial intelligence and ethical frameworks while revealing comparatively less developed thematic areas. The study highlights the importance of integrating Islamic ethical principles, particularly trustworthiness, justice, accountability, and public welfare, into contemporary technological governance. These findings contribute to the literature by providing a systematic understanding of the field's intellectual landscape and identifying potential directions for future interdisciplinary research on responsible artificial intelligence, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, and sustainable digital innovation.

items.title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

items.title: Key Aspects of Eric Miller's Work on Socio-Technical Systems
items.abstract: This part examines Eric Miller’s contribution to the development and application of socio-technical systems (STS) theory within the Tavistock Institute tradition. Building on foundational studies of British coal mining by Trist and Bamforth, Miller advanced the understanding that organizations comprise interdependent social and technical systems whose misalignment produces inefficiency, low morale, and resistance to change. He argued that effective organizational design depends on recognizing organizations as open systems embedded in dynamic environments and on addressing human, structural, and technological factors simultaneously. Central to Miller’s approach was the principle of joint optimization, which holds that neither technical efficiency nor social well-being can be prioritized in isolation. He emphasized participative work design, advocating the involvement of employees in shaping new technologies and processes so that work systems support task performance, autonomy, and collaboration. This perspective informed his support for autonomous and semi-autonomous work groups, demonstrating that responsibility, discretion, and meaningful roles enhance motivation, learning, and innovation. Miller also stressed adaptability and environmental fit, arguing that resilient organizations require flexible structures capable of responding to technological, economic, and social change. As a consultant, he applied STS through action research, positioning the consultant as a facilitator of organizational learning rather than a technical expert. His legacy endures in contemporary organizational practices, such as agile methods, self-managing teams, and human-centred design, where balancing system performance with human experience remains a central challenge.

items.title: Knowledge producers or mere curators? A critical review of student learning and assignment dynamics in the era of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the university landscape offers unprecedented efficiency and speed, radically transforming how students access information and fulfill their academic responsibilities. However, this instantaneous convenience gives rise to a critical shift: do contemporary students remain autonomous knowledge producers, or have they been reduced to mere curators who synthesize and rearrange content from digital repositories? This paper critically examines the dynamics of student learning and assignment completion amidst the expanding AI ecosystem. Employing a reflective-critical approach, the article highlights the paradox of digital efficiency—which accelerates academic processes on one hand, yet risks diminishing critical depth, intellectual autonomy, and student creativity on the other. The analysis reveals that the relationship between students and AI is not merely instrumental; rather, it actively reshapes structural study habits, demanding a profound pedagogical redefinition to ensure that university institutions preserve the fundamental essence of knowledge creation.

items.title: La performance de la logistique hospitalière : un levier stratégique de transformation des hôpitaux publics
items.abstract: Résumé La logistique hospitalière (approvisionnement, gestion des stocks, circuit du médicament, distribution interne, transport et déchets) reste souvent traitée comme une simple fonction de soutien, alors qu’elle conditionne la disponibilité des ressources au point de soins. Cet article vise à repositionner cette fonction comme un levier stratégique de transformation des hôpitaux publics. Il s’appuie sur une revue intégrative de la littérature publiée entre 2004 et 2025 (PubMed et moteur de recherche académique Consensus, complétés par une recherche sur le web), centrée sur les établissements publics et sur les contextes africains et marocain, et mobilise trois cadres théoriques : l’approche sociotechnique, le New Public Management et le Balanced Scorecard. L’analyse d’un corpus de 21 publications fait ressortir trois constats. La performance logistique s’organise autour de trois dimensions rarement traitées ensemble : l’efficience économique, l’efficacité opérationnelle et la qualité perçue. Les indicateurs utilisés sont nombreux mais peu harmonisés ; les revues récentes en recensent des dizaines, à dominante financière. Enfin, le Balanced Scorecard reste peu mobilisé dans les hôpitaux publics des pays à revenu faible et intermédiaire, et le vécu des patients et des personnels y est peu pris en compte. L’article propose un modèle intégrateur et un tableau de bord logistique à quatre perspectives, adapté à la réforme du système de santé marocain engagée par la loi-cadre n° 06-22. Mots clés : Logistique hospitalière, Performance, Chaîne d’approvisionnement, Hôpital public, Balanced Scorecard, New Public Management, Maroc. Abstract Hospital logistics (procurement, inventory management, medication circuit, internal distribution, transport and waste) is still often treated as a mere support function, although it determines the availability of resources at the point of care. This article aims to reposition this function as a strategic lever for transforming public hospitals. It draws on an integrative review of literature published between 2004 and 2025 (PubMed and the Consensus academic search engine, supplemented by a web search), focusing on public facilities and on African and Moroccan contexts, and mobilises three theoretical frameworks: the sociotechnical approach, New Public Management and the Balanced Scorecard. The analysis of a corpus of 21 publications yields three findings. Logistics performance is structured around three dimensions that are rarely addressed together: economic efficiency, operational effectiveness and perceived quality. The indicators in use are numerous but poorly harmonised; recent reviews list dozens of them, mostly financial. Finally, the Balanced Scorecard remains little used in public hospitals in low- and middle-income countries, where the experience of patients and staff is seldom considered. The article proposes an integrative model and a four-perspective logistics scorecard adapted to the reform of the Moroccan health system initiated by framework law No. 06-22. items.title: Large language medicine needs a foundation, not only a frontier
items.abstract: At the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly this year, more than 150 official statements on data, digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) were delivered by 74 countries and 10 regional blocs, alongside 42 side events, and over 30 Ministers of Health affirming digital transformation as a core feature of resilient health systems. The through line was consistent across every region: countries are calling for concerted global leadership towards shared standards and clear governance to validate, benchmark, and regulate AI in health.Sustainable, effective AI requires an ecosystem to function, and often carries real risks to data sovereignty, privacy, and equity. AI trained on incomplete data, tested in narrow settings, or deployed without attention to bias and local context can reproduce, and even amplify, the very inequities it aims to close. It is against this backdrop that we read the lead article by Guni et al. on "large language medicine (1)." We share the authors' optimism but sharpen their central question: not whether generative and multimodal AI will reshape medicine, but how we build the scaffolding that ensures the reshaping happens safely, equitably, and sustainably.Deep learning, generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and connected agentic systems promise both incremental and transformative change across diagnostics, disease management, surveillance, prevention, and drug discovery. Yet, as Guni et al. candidly note, today's clinically mature, regulator-approved tools remain predominantly diagnostic and built on older machine learning architectures. LLMs have not yet crossed into routine practice; interconnected agentic systems are being introduced only in a fraction of cutting-edge facilities. Health systems and clinical medicine, although a rich proving ground for technical experimentation and innovation, are also understandably cautious and risk averse. The principles of evidence-based medicine further solidify the need for requisite, repeated, and rigorous demonstration of efficacy before well-established practices are altered. Some Author 1 et al. Short title/running header 4 critique this caution as innovation recalcitrance; given the duty of care in health, it is better understood as the scientific scrutiny that any clinical tool, however heavily promoted, should be expected to survive.An AI solution does not scale on its own; it scales when an ecosystem for scale exists or is built around it. This includes clear regulatory capacity and governance, strong health information systems, and trained health personnel. We posit that a key element of that enabling foundation is digital public infrastructure for health. Some of the most durable gains come not from what makes headlines but from the unglamorous parts of the system no one photographs: the unique identifiers and information exchanges, the semantic standards which allow systems to interoperate, powering supply chains that keep essential medicines on the shelf, and persistent records that follow a patient across facilities within a health system to maintain continuity of care. Countries that adopted monolithic, donor-funded digital health tools have already seen those systems collapse when funding shifted; language models deployed as parallel silos, disconnected from a shared reference architecture, risk repeating that failure at greater speed and scale. Technology-neutral reference architectures, developed collaboratively across health and telecommunications agencies and built on open standards, offer a map for where these foundations should sit (2). AI cannot pervade "every aspect of medicine," as Guni et al. envision, without an underlying layer of high-quality data structured for interoperability, disciplined evaluation protocols, and the systems analysis required to introduce AI into existing clinical workflows. Experimental systems may be introduced into clinical practice, but without clear proof points and performance benchmarks, their transition from pilot to clinical standard will likely be slow and inequitable. Ministries and hospital systems are already experiencing a glut of vendors promising impressive solutions to long-standing challenges, often without the accompanying (3,4), or countries with the least regulatory capacity will simply import externally reviewed systems without local ownership. Regulatory sandboxes, such as the United Kingdom's AI Airlock, which allows supervised testing of AI tools that fit no existing device category (5), remain an underused bridge between principle and practice. Harmonization does not mean uniformity; it means enough common evidentiary ground that a safety finding in one country still holds in another, since the models themselves will cross borders faster than any single regulator's jurisdiction can follow. Language, disease burden, health system maturity, and data availability vary enormously; a model validated in one setting cannot be assumed safe in another. Multi-institutional, privacy-preserving evaluation designed into deployment from the start, not bolted on afterward, should be the norm, particularly for populations already under-represented in training data. This brings us to what authentic inclusion in AI design actually looks like. It is not access to a shared global model. It is each country's ability to shape a model on the data of its own population, keep it under its own governance, regulate it according to its own values and context, and operate it through a health workforce with the capacity to evaluate its outputs. A ministry that cannot inspect a model, audit its performance against its own population's outcomes, or withdraw it from clinical use does not exercise meaningful oversight.Sovereignty in this context is not isolation; it is knowing where data sit, who processes them, under whose law, and on what terms access can be revoked. Without populationrepresentative data, locally grounded regulation, and a trained workforce able to question and override the system where necessary, the populations furthest behind will bear the greatest exposure to model failure, precisely because they are least represented in training data and least resourced to identify when a system is underperforming. This is a critical moment to set a shared direction for how AI in health is governed. items.title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
items.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.

items.title: Leader-Follower Hierarchical Role Effects on Individual and Shared Trust in Mixed Human-AI Teams
items.abstract: Human-AI Teams (HATs) are evolving into increasingly complex multi-human multi-agent structures, including those with hierarchical leadership and role accountability. Conventionally, humans have primarily taken leadership positions, directing and supervising autonomous agents. However, emerging HAT contexts now enable humans to assume a wider range of hierarchical roles within teams, including both leader and follower positions. Despite these developments, empirical research on non-dyadic HATs remains limited, leaving important questions regarding trust and teamwork in complex team structures largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate how hierarchical roles differentially shape trust in AI teammates and trust in the team as a whole, as well as how role-based trust divergence associates with overall team outcomes. We find that trust varies significantly by the trustor’s role, yet shared trust and reduced trust divergence across teammates are critical for better team performance. Accordingly, it is important to support shared team cognition and mitigate trust divergence.

items.title: Learning from Physical Experience:Context-Space Adaptation for Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

items.title: Learning Integrated School Model: Impacts of ISO 14001–9001–45001 on School Culture, Student Behavior and Sustainable Educational Governance
items.abstract: Educational institutions are increasingly regarded as environments where regulatory expectations, quality development, safety awareness, and sustainability come together. This study investigates how the joint implementation of ISO 14001 (environmental management), ISO 9001 (quality management), and ISO 45001 (occupational health and safety) influences school culture, student behaviour, and stakeholder participation in different school settings in Düzce, Türkiye, including preschool, primary, lower secondary, and special education institutions. The Learning Integrated School Model (LISM) is introduced as a conceptual framework that interprets these standards as interconnected components of an organisational learning structure rather than separate technical requirements. The research was designed as a qualitative case study. Semi-structured interviews with 10 school administrators and 18 teachers were conducted through maximum variation sampling to reflect diverse implementation experiences. Interview data were analysed by thematic content analysis, and reliability was reinforced through dual coding, participant confirmation, and expert feedback. The findings suggest that integrated management systems contribute to environmentally aware and safety-oriented behavioural patterns among students and support more reflective planning and monitoring in instructional processes. They also encourage cooperation and shared ownership among staff, while sustainability-based behaviours extend the school’s influence into family environments. At the same time, documentation workload, time constraints, resource limitations, and differing levels of engagement present challenges that shape the continuity of these systems. It is concluded that the Learning Integrated School Model creates a continuous learning cycle by aligning environmental, quality, and safety practices, thereby reinforcing sustainability-oriented school culture. More effective digital documentation tools, expanded role-based professional development, and structured networks for sharing implementation experiences may strengthen integration efforts. The study offers a perspective that views integrated management systems as contributors to educational transformation, providing insights for both practitioners and policy development.

items.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Career Development: The Effect of AI Use Intention on Graduate Employability Through Career Adaptability and Job Search Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: Background: Fresh graduates face an increasingly difficult school-to-work transition, while artificial intelligence (AI) has become a routine study and job-search companion; yet how the intention to use AI translates into employability, and through which mechanisms, remains unclear. Objective: Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study tests whether behavioral intention to use AI is associated with self-perceived graduate employability directly and indirectly through career adaptability and job search self-efficacy, and whether AI self-efficacy and AI trust moderate these paths. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey of 612 Indonesian fresh graduates who use AI for career preparation was analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: AI use intention positively predicted career adaptability (β = 0.305) and job search self-efficacy (β = 0.249), and both resources predicted self-perceived employability. The indirect paths through both resources were significant, and a direct effect of AI use intention on employability remained, indicating partial mediation. AI self-efficacy and AI trust showed significant main effects on their resources, while the interaction-related indirect effects were not significant. Conclusion: AI use intention is associated with self-perceived employability through career adaptability and job search self-efficacy. The cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Educational institutions and career-service units may use these findings to inform structured AI-supported occupational exploration, skills-gap analysis, résumé refinement, and interview rehearsal, while encouraging critical verification of AI outputs.

items.title: Linguistic and Stylistic Over-Elaboration in AI-Permitted Arabic Writing Tasks: Evidence from Beginner Learners
items.abstract: This study examines linguistic and stylistic over-elaboration in beginner Arabic writing produced during a classroom task permitting generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and electronic translation. The study emerged from an Arabic language course involving undergraduate accounting students at Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM), Terengganu Branch, Malaysia. Students were instructed to write a simple birthday invitation addressed to friends, using accessible vocabulary and including specified invitation elements. During the review of approximately 100 submissions, the instructor observed recurring instances of vocabulary, courtesy expressions, and sentence formulations that appeared more sophisticated or formal than expected for the learners' proficiency and the task's communicative purpose. Adopting an exploratory qualitative approach, the study draws on these professional classroom observations, supplemented by the direct examination of three available invitation texts. The analysis considers lexical overreach, stylistic over-elaboration, unnecessary syntactic complexity, register mismatch, and learner-level appropriateness. The findings highlight a pedagogical distinction between linguistic correctness and the suitability of written expression for a beginner's level and communicative situation. They also suggest that apparently sophisticated writing should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of independent linguistic proficiency. Because individual tool use and writing processes were not documented, the study does not attribute particular expressions to GenAI or establish causal effects.

items.title: LLM Recommenders Produce Demographic Inequality Through Content Preferences
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into systems that rank and recommend online content. We examine how this shift can produce demographic inequality in whose voices are surfaced. Using 10,000 Twitter/X posts written by 1,000 survey respondents and linked to verified self-reported characteristics across nine demographic attributes, we conduct a controlled recommendation experiment across three LLM providers, six recommendation objectives, and five levels of contextual information. By varying whether models receive post text alone, platform metadata, or explicit author demographics, we isolate three pathways to unequal recommendation: preferences for demographically patterned content, reliance on unequal engagement signals, and direct use of disclosed identity. We find that demographic inequality emerges from text alone. Models consistently favour longer, more negative, and more opinionated posts, particularly those concerning news and social issues, producing systematic differences in the demographic composition of recommended authors. Platform metadata generally amplifies these inequalities, while explicitly disclosing authors' demographic characteristics produces little additional change. Recommendation objectives mainly affect the magnitude of these patterns: controversial framing intensifies both content and demographic skew, whereas popularity-oriented framing dampens it, although for some attributes - most notably age - the objective can also reverse which group is favoured. LLM-based recommenders can therefore reproduce demographic inequality by proxy, not through explicit demographic targeting, but through preferences for content and engagement signals already structured by social inequality.

items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine the systemic tensions between traditional library values and rapid technological adoption in 2026. Design/methodology/approach The paper synthesizes findings from recent industry reports including Marshall Breeding’s, 2026 Library Systems Report and analysis of landmark legal cases on e-lending. items.title: Logged Is Not Done: Verifiable AI Operations for the EU AI Act Era (Part 01 of 15)
items.abstract: Abstract As AI agents start to act in European critical infrastructure (telecom networks, payment systems, cloud platforms and industrial robots), a recurring gap appears. A system can log that an operation was authorized and acknowledged, yet still be unable to show that the evidence behind it was current, or that the reported result matches what actually happened. This gap matters to obligations under the EU AI Act, including: risk management (Article 9); record-keeping and logging (Article 12); human oversight (Article 14); accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15); post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting (Articles 72–73). This publication presents the foundational part of a 15-part technical series, also submitted as an IETF Internet-Draft. It defines a vendor-neutral evidence-consistency framework built on these elements: every consequential operation receives a stable identity and a declared verification objective; each observation carries its provenance, resource generation, time interval and clock uncertainty; domain-specific checks produce a scoped three-valued result: SUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED or UNRESOLVED. UNRESOLVED is a first-class outcome. Missing or stale evidence is recorded honestly rather than reported as success, which gives auditors, oversight personnel and incident investigators a reconstructable decision record. The framework keeps verification separate from authority. A positive result never grants permission to act; any consequential effect stays under a separate, accountable control boundary. Acknowledgement, completion, physical outcome and financial settlement are reconciled as independent evidence. A three-layer architecture keeps shared evidence semantics apart from twelve domain profiles: radio access and network incident recovery; telecom sessions and charging; hardware and DMA command paths; multi-agent negotiation and asynchronous tools; robotics and physical safety; multilingual emergency instructions; browser agents and agent migration; autonomous commerce; accelerator reset. The material is also relevant to engineering work under NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, DORA and the Machinery Regulation. The PDF includes: a reader's summary with diagrams; an analytical latency and capacity model with a measurement plan; 12 proposed verification tests; threat and edge-case profiles; a searchable catalogue of 639 engineering mechanisms. The document describes technical mechanisms and makes no legal-compliance, certification or conformity claim.

items.title: Long Term Impact of Occupational Exposure to Fine Particulate Matter on the Incidence of Rare Histological Subtypes of Lung Cancer
items.abstract: Chronic occupational exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) has been linked to an elevated risk of respiratory diseases, but the association between this exposure and the incidence of rare histological types of lung cancer has not yet been sufficiently studied. The current retrospective cohort study assesses the association between cumulative occupational exposure to PM2.5 and the incidence of rare lung cancer subtypes among industrial workers. Information on occupational health, occupational exposure measurements, and regional cancer registry data obtained in 2006-2023 have been used for the analysis. This study covers 6,500 employees of mining, construction, and metalworking industries. Exposures of individuals were determined from PM₂.₅ measurements in the workplace and the use of job-exposure matrices. Rare lung cancer events were documented from histopathology reports and categorized based on standardized tumor classification. Over a median follow-up of 13.4 years, 226 lung cancer events were documented, with 39 rare histology types (17.3%). The highest PM₂.₅ exposure group had an increased risk of rare lung cancer compared to the lowest PM₂.₅ exposure group (HR = 1.79; 95%CI: 1.18–2.71; p = 0.004). From the continuous exposure model, there was increased risk for each 10 µg/m³ increase in cumulative exposure to PM₂.₅. It can be concluded that long-term exposure to PM₂.₅ at workplaces increases the incidence of rare lung cancer subtypes.

items.title: Machine Learning, Foundation Models, Skills, and Agents in the Energy Industry: A Systematic, Evidence-Graded Survey
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in energy is reported far more often than it is deployed, and the evidence that would let an operator tell the difference is scattered across literatures that do not cite each other. This survey assembles it. We grade 678 claims drawn from 883 evidence cards over 455 sources across four pillars (classical and deep machine learning, foundation models, capability packaging and agents) and the whole value chain, applying one deployment ladder (demo, pilot, field trial and production) to every system. Three findings recur. First, the subfields differ in evaluation regime, not in any measured model capability: the earliest petroleum large-language-model benchmarks found date from 2026, the power sector’s from 2024, and none of them reports a human-expert baseline, so none of their scores can be read as expertlevel. Second, in this corpus, two places differ: in drilling automation and artificial lift, software writes setpoints to field equipment with no human approving each action, yet the artificial-lift system with the broadest such authority contains no machine learning, and every reinforcement-learning system here that actuates does so in a simulator, not on a well. Third, the sources in this corpus rarely measure the field’s own adoption: no Tier A source found reports an adoption rate, a pilot-to-production conversion ratio, a total cost of ownership, or a post-mortem of a cancelled programme, and 63 claims here are formally evidenced absences. The survey reports its own failures, among them a retracted absence claim, a measured skew in its own corpus and seven source caches holding the wrong document.

items.title: Making argumentative work visible in GenAI-mediated assessment: an exploratory LLM simulation and questionnaire study in university ideological and political education
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI weakens the correspondence between the final text of an assignment and the argumentative work involved in producing it. This study examined how task structure and AI-use instructions shape evidence use, engagement with objections, and revision in university ideological and political education. Methods An LLM simulation crossed three task formats—position essays, evidence-integration memoranda, and follow-up-and-revision defense tasks—with three AI-use scenarios—simulated no-AI, responsible collaboration, and concealed ghostwriting. Two raters coded 148 generated texts with the Textual Response Artifact Scoring Index (TRASI), and an anonymous questionnaire collected 268 evaluations of 27 selected texts. Results Responsible collaboration produced the highest overall rubric score ( M = 3.32). Evidence-integration memoranda ( M = 3.16) and follow-up-and-revision defenses ( M = 3.10) exceeded position essays ( M = 2.63). Position essays varied most across the three AI-use scenarios, whereas the memorandum and defense showed narrower differences because their instructions already required source explanation or response and revision. Questionnaire participants distinguished the same task functions: memoranda were rated highest for source–claim linkage, and defenses for counterargument response and revision explanation. Open-ended responses associated evidence integration, comparison of reasons, and revision with thinking, while formulaic structure, over-polished expression, and generic abstraction were associated with AI-like writing. Discussion Task structure and AI-use instructions were functionally complementary. Structured tasks elicited source explanation or challenge and revision directly, so responsible collaboration added its largest contribution in the general position essay. GenAI-mediated assessment can therefore be designed around the argumentative decisions that writers are required to document.

items.title: Mapping the Intellectual Architecture of Education for Sustainable Development in Higher Education: A Bibliometric and AI-Assisted Thematic Synthesis
items.abstract: Background Despite the substantial growth of research on Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) in higher education, the field remains characterized by geographic concentration, methodological constraints, and conceptual fragmentation between established competence frameworks and emerging demands such as climate literacy and green skills. No prior review has simultaneously mapped the bibliometric architecture and conducted an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted inductive thematic synthesis of this domain. Methods A dual-method design integrated bibliometric network analysis—co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence—with AI-assisted inductive thematic synthesis. A total of 442 peer-reviewed documents were retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and ERIC (2015–2026) through systematic multi-database search, deduplication, and PICO-adapted relevance screening evaluated by a specialized multi-rater panel (Fleiss’ κ=0.55 – 0.69 , 98.4% unanimous agreement on the retained corpus). Thematic extraction was performed using two complementary large language model architectures (Qwen3-235B and DeepSeek V3.2), governed by a stringent verification protocol achieving a 92.0% alignment score; 37 hallucination flags were audited and corrected via human expert review. Results The corpus exhibits substantial and accelerated scientific expansion since 2019 ( R2=0.91 for exponential fit; compound annual growth rate of 18.4%), with Spain, the United Kingdom, and Germany accounting for over one-third of output. Five thematic clusters emerged: curriculum integration, transformative pedagogies, institutional and faculty roles, sustainability literacy and behavioral outcomes, and digital innovation. Surveys and case studies dominate research designs (37.7%), while experimental approaches represent only 4.0% of the corpus. Green skills and climate literacy remain conceptually peripheral despite their policy urgency, institutional collaboration is fragmented (20.3% of institutions isolated), and faculty populations are understudied (7.0%) relative to students (32.7%). Fifty-six knowledge gaps were identified across structural, declared, and emergent categories, with methods-by-concepts coverage reaching 64.0%. Conclusions The field would benefit from a methodological transition toward longitudinal and experimental designs, enhanced visibility of Global South scholarship (contextualizing database indexing constraints), systematic pedagogical theorization of simulation-based approaches, and deliberate cross-institutional consortia to transition from conceptual proliferation to evidence-based pedagogical science.

items.title: Marital Status, Ergonomic Challenges, and Academic Performance among University Students in Nigeria
items.abstract: Ergonomic challenges in university learning environments are increasingly recognized as important factors influencing student health and academic performance.However, there is limited evidence on how these challenges interact with socio-demographic factors such as marital status, particularly in low-and middle-income countries.This cross-sectional study was conducted among 352 students at the University of Calabar, Nigeria.Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire that incorporated elements of the Standard Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire.Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and logistic regression were applied to examine the relationship between marital status, cumulative ergonomic challenges, and academic performance.Married students accounted for 2.56% of the study population.Commonly reported ergonomic challenges included musculoskeletal strain, poor lighting, non-adjustable furniture, and inadequate learning infrastructure.A moderate positive relationship was observed between cumulative ergonomic burden and academic performance impairment (r = 0.508), although this was not statistically significant.In the unadjusted analysis, married female students had higher exposure to ergonomic stressors and poorer academic outcomes compared to their male counterparts (OR = 2.00).However, after adjusting for ergonomic burden, this relationship reversed (AOR = 0.533), suggesting that the observed differences were largely driven by unequal exposure to environmental stressors rather than gender.Ergonomic challenges are a significant but often overlooked determinant of academic performance among university students.These findings highlight the need for institution-wide ergonomic interventions, particularly for vulnerable groups, to improve learning conditions, reduce physical strain, and support better academic outcomes.

items.title: Masculinidades digitais e educação midiática: : vulnerabilidade psicossocial e prevenção da hostilidade online em contextos formativos, uma revisão de escopo
items.abstract: Digital media constitute relevant spaces for the socialization of masculinities, where gender norms, belonging, vulnerability, and hostility may be reproduced, negotiated, or contested. This scoping review aimed to map the contributions, strategies, and possibilities of media literacy for recognizing, problematizing, and preventing online hostility related to the construction of masculinities among adolescents and young people in educational contexts. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and the PRISMA-ScR framework. Fifty-three articles published between 2021 and 2026 were included, identified through SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, and the CAPES Journals Portal; data were extracted using a standardized matrix and synthesized descriptively and thematically. The synthesis resulted in five axes: digital masculinities; education, intervention, and prevention; hostile communities and radicalization; vulnerability, belonging, and recognition; and online hostility and masculine norms. Media literacy was explicitly addressed in nine studies and involved gender perspectives, critical analysis of influencers, gender disinformation, algorithmic awareness, consent, empathy, and peer support. Only two interventions were evaluated. Preventive strategies should therefore integrate masculine socialization, belonging, vulnerability, and sociotechnical mediation, while further intervention, longitudinal, and youth-centered studies are needed.

items.title: Mathematics Outcomes and Creative Metacognition in Primary Students: A Quasi-Experimental Study Using AI-Generated Explanations
items.abstract: This exploration examines the impact of supplementary AI-generated explanatory materials on foundational mathematics learning and creative metacognition in primary education. The study followed a quantitative, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with a nonequivalent control group. Fourth-grade classes in five schools were assigned to conditions at the classroom level: an intervention group receiving AI-facilitated handouts (n = 135) and a control group using programmatic textbooks (n = 128). Students in the experimental condition received eight supplementary lessons featuring paper-based handouts. These handouts presented explanations, examples, and illustrations of new mathematical topics generated by a large language model (Gemini 2.5 Pro), prompted the inclusion of age-appropriate content and a dedicated section encouraging creative metacognition (reflection and novel idea generation). Baseline equivalence was confirmed. The outcomes assessed included single-digit mental arithmetic, multidigit calculation, arithmetic word problem-solving, and creative metacognition, which were analyzed via multilevel or robust linear modeling accounting for classroom clustering. The results indicated no statistically significant differences between groups on single-digit mental arithmetic tasks. However, students who received AI-generated materials showed significantly greater improvement in multidigit calculation tasks and one-step word problem-solving than did the control group. No significant difference was found for multistep word problems. The intervention group also presented a substantially greater increase in creative metacognition scores than did the control group. The findings provide preliminary quasi-experimental evidence that curated, static AI-generated explanations, when designed to include metacognitive prompts, may be associated with greater gains in specific procedural and applied mathematical skills and creative metacognition among fourth-grade students under the conditions studied. This approach illustrates how generative AI can be leveraged as an authoring tool to supplement standard instruction and cultivate higher-order cognitive skills in young learners.
